nameStory: The margined madtom gets its name from the distinctive dark edges or 'margins' on its fins that help distinguish it from other madtoms. The 'madtom' part of the name comes from these small catfish's habit of inflicting painful stings with their pectoral fin spines when handled - enough to make someone 'mad' with pain!
description: The margined madtom is a tiny freshwater catfish, typically growing only 3-4 inches long, making it one of New England's smallest catfish species. Like all catfish, it has smooth, scaleless skin and sensitive whisker-like barbels around its mouth for finding food in murky water. Its body is elongated and somewhat flattened, with a mottled brown and yellow coloration that helps it blend perfectly with rocky stream bottoms. This secretive little fish is extremely rare in New England, with only one confirmed observation in the region.

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Look for dark margins or edges on the dorsal, anal, and tail fins - these black borders are the key identifying feature and feel slightly thicker than the rest of the fin membrane

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small for a catfish, rarely exceeding 4 inches in length - about the size of a large minnow with a stocky, robust build

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Elongated but somewhat flattened body with smooth, slippery skin that feels like wet velvet - no scales anywhere on the body

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Mottled brown and yellowish coloration with darker blotches that create excellent camouflage against sandy and rocky stream bottoms

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small, terminal mouth with four barbels on the chin and four around the upper jaw that feel like soft, flexible whiskers

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found hiding under rocks and debris in clear, fast-flowing streams with rocky or gravel bottoms - rarely seen in open water

habitat: Margined madtoms prefer clear, fast-flowing streams and small rivers with rocky or gravel bottoms where they can hide under stones and debris. They need well-oxygenated water and are typically found in riffles and shallow runs. In New England, this species is at the extreme northern edge of its range and is exceptionally rare.

seasonality.spring: Most active during spawning season when males may be found guarding nests under flat rocks or logs. Water temperatures warming above 60°F trigger increased activity.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most likely to be encountered, though still extremely secretive and nocturnal in their habits.
seasonality.fall: Activity decreases as water temperatures cool, and they become even more reclusive, spending more time hidden under cover.
seasonality.winter: Nearly inactive in cold water, remaining hidden under rocks and logs in deeper pools with minimal movement.

funFact: Despite being only 3-4 inches long, margined madtoms pack venomous spines in their pectoral fins that can deliver an extremely painful sting - some people describe it as worse than a bee sting and lasting for hours!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the stonecat, another small catfish, but stonecats lack the distinctive dark fin margins and are typically more uniformly colored. Remember: margined madtom has dark-edged fins like it's been outlined with a black marker.
contextualKnowledge: The single observation count in New England reflects this species' rarity in the region - it's primarily a southeastern species that barely reaches into southern New England. Any sighting would be considered significant from a conservation perspective.
compareHints: Compared to its closest relative the stonecat, the margined madtom is distinguished by those characteristic dark fin margins and typically more mottled coloration. Stonecats are more uniformly yellowish-brown and lack the distinct black edges on their fins. Both species are small and secretive, but only the margined madtom has that telltale 'outlined' appearance to its fins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relative the margined madtom, the stonecat prefers faster-moving water and has a more streamlined body shape.
